myth-001.summary: King of the Olympian gods, who wields the thunderbolt as his weapon.
facts: The planet Jupiter is named after his Roman counterpart, Jupiter.
The Statue of Zeus at Olympia was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
stories: When the war against the Titans had dragged on for ten years with no end in sight, Zeus freed the Cyclops brothers and the hundred-handed giants who had been imprisoned in Tartarus. In gratitude, the Cyclops brothers forged a thunderbolt for Zeus, a trident for Poseidon, and a helmet for Hades. Thunderbolt in hand, Zeus crushed the Titans and became king of the gods.

After locking the Titans away in Tartarus, Zeus drew lots with his brothers Poseidon and Hades to divide up the world. Zeus won the wide sky, Poseidon the gray sea, and Hades the gloomy underworld. The earth and lofty Mount Olympus were to be shared by all three, and Zeus, lord of the sky, ruled the world as king of the gods.

Zeus fell for Europa, a Phoenician princess, and approached her as she played on the seashore, disguised as a bull as white as snow. When Europa, trusting the gentle bull, climbed onto its back, Zeus plunged straight into the sea and carried her all the way to Crete. There Europa bore Zeus three sons: Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthus.

myth-002.summary: Queen of the gods and goddess who protects marriage and the home.
facts: The English word June most likely comes from her Roman name, Juno.
She is said to have set the hundred eyes of the slain Argus into the peacock’s tail.
stories: Suspicious of clouds that had blanketed the earth in broad daylight, Hera came down to look, and Zeus, to avoid being caught, turned his lover Io into a pure white heifer. Seeing through the trick, Hera asked for the heifer as a gift and, once she had it, set the hundred-eyed Argus to guard it day and night. Even after Argus was slain, Hera sent a dreadful goddess of vengeance to chase Io across the whole world.

Jealous of Semele, the princess of Thebes who was carrying Zeus’s child, Hera disguised herself as Semele’s old nurse and paid her a visit. She urged Semele to test her lover: if he was truly Zeus, he should show himself in his true form, just as he did when he came to Hera. Zeus, who had sworn by the river Styx to grant Semele anything, had no choice but to appear with his thunderbolts, and Semele was burned to ashes; only her unborn baby, Dionysus, survived, growing to term inside Zeus’s thigh.

When Zeus boasted that a child of his bloodline born that day would rule over all his neighbors, Hera made him seal the words with an oath. She then hurried down to Argos and brought on the labor of Sthenelus’s wife, only seven months pregnant, while holding back Alcmene’s delivery. So Eurystheus, born first, became king, and Heracles was later forced to perform grueling labors at his command.

myth-003.summary: Zeus’s older brother, who can shake both sea and land with a single trident.
facts: The planet Neptune takes its name from his Roman name, Neptune.
He was said to have created the first horse by striking a rock with his trident, so he was also worshipped as the god of horses.
stories: When Odysseus blinded the one-eyed giant Polyphemus and escaped, the giant prayed to his father, Poseidon, for revenge. Poseidon did not kill Odysseus, but he kept him wandering the seas, unable to reach home, and when Odysseus set out on a raft, Poseidon raised a storm that smashed it to pieces. Only ten years after leaving Troy did Odysseus finally set foot on his home island of Ithaca.

Taking human form, Poseidon and Apollo agreed to work for wages for a year under Laomedon, king of Troy. Poseidon built the broad, beautiful walls that ringed the city, but when the year was up, the king refused to pay and even threatened to sell the two gods as slaves on a distant island. Enraged, Poseidon sent a sea monster to attack the people in the fields, and he bore Troy a deep grudge ever after.

Poseidon quarreled with Hera over the land of Argos, and the river gods Inachus, Cephissus, and Asterion were called in to judge. When the three river gods awarded the land to Hera, a furious Poseidon dried up their waters. That is why, according to the traveler Pausanias, these rivers flow only after it rains.

myth-004.summary: Earth goddess who makes the grain grow.
facts: Her grief at losing her daughter to the underworld is told as the origin of the seasons.
Breakfast cereal gets its name from her Roman name, Ceres.
stories: Learning that her daughter had been dragged off to the underworld, Demeter left Olympus and shut herself away alone in her temple at Eleusis. She hid the seeds in the ground, so for a whole year nothing sprouted; people went hungry, and even the offerings to the gods were about to run out. The gods came one after another bearing gifts, but Demeter would not budge, and she let grain grow in the fields again only after Zeus sent Hermes to bring her daughter back.

While searching for her daughter, Demeter disguised herself as an old woman and became a nursemaid in the royal palace at Eleusis. Hoping to make the infant prince immortal, she secretly placed him in the hearth fire every night, but the queen saw it and screamed, and the plan was ruined. Revealing her true form, Demeter ordered a temple built in her honor, and this was the beginning of the Eleusinian Mysteries.

When Erysichthon of Thessaly took twenty servants to cut down a great tree in a sacred grove, Demeter appeared in the form of her priestess Nicippe and urged him to stop. When Erysichthon retorted that he would use the tree to build a banquet hall, the goddess revealed her true form, so huge that her feet stood on the ground while her head touched Olympus. Demeter then cursed him with a terrible hunger that no amount of food could ever satisfy.

myth-005.summary: Goddess of wisdom, born fully armed from her father’s head.
facts: Her bird, the owl, appears on the back of Greece’s 1-euro coin.
The Parthenon on the Acropolis was a temple dedicated to her.
stories: When the gods were each choosing a city where they would be worshipped, Athena found herself competing with Poseidon for the land of Attica. Poseidon struck the middle of the Acropolis with his trident and made a spring of seawater gush forth, but Athena planted an olive tree beside it. When King Cecrops testified that Athena had planted her tree first, the twelve gods awarded the land to the goddess, and Athena named the city Athens after herself.

When the Giants stormed the heavens, hurling boulders and blazing oak trees, Athena fought alongside the other gods. As the giant Enceladus fled in fear, Athena lifted the entire island of Sicily and hurled it down on top of him, crushing him. Ever since, Enceladus has lain pinned beneath Mount Etna, breathing out fire, and the island is said to shake whenever he stirs.

Athena bored holes in a piece of boxwood and made the first flute, and its music was lovely to hear. But when she saw her reflection in clear water, her cheeks were puffed out most unbecomingly from playing. Deciding the skill was not worth the price, the goddess threw the flute away, and later the satyr Marsyas picked it up and challenged Apollo to a music contest.

myth-006.summary: God of light, who plays the lyre and delivers prophecies.
facts: At his temple in Delphi, he gave oracles through the mouth of his priestess, the Pythia.
The US Apollo program, which sent the first humans to the Moon in 1969, was named after him.
stories: After laying the foundations of his temple at the foot of Mount Parnassus, Apollo shot a huge she-serpent with his bow that had been killing people near a nearby spring. The monster writhed in agony and died, and its body rotted where it lay under the sun. So the place was called Pytho, from a word meaning “to rot,” and Apollo came to be known as the god of Pytho.

When Apollo mocked Eros’s skill with the bow, Eros shot Apollo with a golden arrow of love and the nymph Daphne with a lead arrow that repels love. As Apollo chased her, Daphne prayed to her father, a river god, and was turned into a laurel tree. Apollo wove a wreath from its leaves to wear and made the laurel his sacred tree.

Having founded his temple at Delphi, Apollo was looking for priests to tend it when he spotted a ship of Cretans crossing the sea to trade. He turned into a huge dolphin and leaped aboard, and while the terrified sailors stood helpless, he drove the ship all the way to the port of Crisa. Revealing his true form, Apollo made them priests of his temple, and from then on he was also called Delphinius, “god of the dolphin.”

myth-007.summary: Goddess of the hunt, who roams the forest with a bow on her back.
facts: The twin of Apollo, she is said to have been born first on the island of Delos and then helped deliver her brother.
NASA’s Artemis lunar program, the successor to the Apollo program, is named after her.
stories: The hunter Actaeon happened to catch sight of Artemis bathing in a forest spring. The furious goddess splashed water on him, and antlers sprouted from his head as his whole body turned into a stag. Actaeon was chased down by his own hunting dogs and torn to death.

Niobe, queen of Thebes, boasted of her many children and claimed she was greater than Leto, who had borne only two. To defend their mother’s honor, Apollo shot down all of Niobe’s sons and Artemis all of her daughters. Left all alone, Niobe turned into a rock on Mount Sipylus, and tears are said to flow from that rock to this day.

Artemis outwitted the giant brothers Otus and Ephialtes, who had threatened to pile mountain upon mountain and storm the heavens. When Otus presumed to make her his wife, the goddess turned into a deer on the island of Naxos and darted between the two brothers. Each eager to hit the deer first, the brothers hurled their spears at each other, and Artemis struck them both down without lifting a finger.

myth-008.summary: Savage god of war, who loves fighting for its own sake.
facts: He was unpopular in Greece but greatly revered in Rome.
The planet Mars and the English month of March both come from his Roman name, Mars.
stories: When Halirrhothius, a son of Poseidon, tried to assault Ares’s daughter Alcippe, Ares caught him in the act and killed him. Poseidon charged Ares with murder, and the twelve gods gathered on a hill in Athens to hold a trial. Ares was acquitted, and because he was the first to be tried there, the hill was called the Hill of Ares, or the Areopagus.

In the Trojan War, Ares and Enyo, goddess of battle, led the Trojan army and drove the Greeks back hard. Taking human form and brandishing an enormous spear, Ares ranged in front of and behind Hector, and at the sight of him even the hero Diomedes shuddered and called for a retreat. Wherever Hector and Ares swept through together, the Greek heroes fell one after another.

When his son Cycnus challenged Heracles, who was on his way to the Hesperides, to single combat, Ares took his son’s side and directed the fight himself. But a thunderbolt flew down from the sky and struck between the two fighters, cutting the duel short. In Hesiod’s poem, Ares, having lost his son, attacks Heracles himself and is driven off with his thigh pierced by Heracles’ spear.

myth-009.summary: Goddess of love and beauty, born from the sea foam.
facts: Her winning of the golden apple set off the chain of events that led to the Trojan War.
The planet Venus takes its English name from her Roman name, Venus.
stories: Aphrodite loved the handsome hunter Adonis dearly and begged him not to chase fierce beasts. But Adonis went hunting anyway and died, gored by a wild boar’s tusk. When the grieving goddess sprinkled his blood with nectar, the drink of the gods, a red anemone bloomed on the spot.

Aphrodite fell for Anchises of Troy, who was herding cattle on Mount Ida, so she adorned herself in her temple on Cyprus and went to him disguised as a mortal maiden. After they had lain together, the goddess revealed her true form and told him he would have a son, who would be raised by the mountain nymphs. The child was named Aeneas, and the goddess sternly warned Anchises never to boast of the affair to anyone.

In the Trojan War, when her son Aeneas was struck down by a stone thrown by Diomedes, Aphrodite wrapped him in her white arms and covered him with a fold of her shining robe. Diomedes chased after her and stabbed her wrist with his spear, and Aphrodite screamed and let go of her son, whom Apollo rescued instead. The wounded goddess borrowed Ares’s chariot and fled to Olympus.

myth-010.summary: Lame blacksmith god who forges the weapons of Olympus.
facts: His temple, standing on a hill above the Agora in Athens, is still nearly intact after more than 2,400 years.
The word volcano comes from his Roman name, Vulcan.
stories: When Achilles lost his armor, his mother, Thetis, went to Hephaestus’s bronze palace and begged him to make new arms for her son. Remembering how Thetis had caught him when he was flung from heaven, Hephaestus set his bellows to work at once. He made a helmet and armor, along with a shield engraved with the sky, the earth, and the sea, a city holding a feast and a city engulfed in war, and even farmers plowing their fields.

Hearing from Helios that his wife, Aphrodite, was secretly meeting Ares, Hephaestus forged chains as fine as a spider web yet impossible to break. He set the chains around the bed and pretended to leave for Lemnos, and when Ares and Aphrodite climbed in, they were caught fast. Hephaestus called the gods together, who roared with laughter, and the pair were set free only after Poseidon guaranteed compensation.

Hera threw the newborn Hephaestus down from Olympus because he was ugly. Raised by sea goddesses, he later sent his mother a golden throne as a gift, and the moment Hera sat down, invisible chains bound her fast. Only after Dionysus got Hephaestus drunk and brought him back to Olympus was Hera finally freed.

myth-011.summary: Messenger of the gods, who carries their news in winged sandals.
facts: In 1902, the US Army Medical Corps adopted his staff, entwined with two snakes, as its insignia.
Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun, takes its English name from his Roman name.
stories: On the day he was born, Hermes slipped out of his cradle and made off with fifty of Apollo’s cattle. He drove them backward to hide their tracks, but he was found out in the end. He soothed Apollo’s anger by giving him a lyre made from a tortoise shell, and the two became close from then on.

When Zeus told him to rescue Io, who had been turned into a heifer, Hermes disguised himself as a herdsman and approached Argus, the hundred-eyed watchman. Playing his reed pipes and telling long stories, Hermes lulled every last one of Argus’s eyes to sleep, though two of them had always stayed open by turns. Then Hermes struck Argus down with his sword, and so, it is said, he earned the epithet Argeiphontes, “slayer of Argus.”

When Circe turned Odysseus’s men into pigs, Hermes appeared before Odysseus as a young man and gave him moly, an herb that would ward off her magic. With a black root and a milk-white flower, the herb was hard for mortals to dig up. Hermes told him that when Circe tried to strike him with her wand, he should draw his sword and rush at her, then make her swear never to harm him again.

myth-012.summary: Wandering god of revelry who teaches people about wine.
facts: At his festival in Athens, contests of tragedy and comedy were held every year.
Bacchus, a Korean energy tonic made by Dong-A Pharmaceutical, is named after his Roman name, Bacchus.
stories: Pirates mistook the young Dionysus for a prince of some kingdom and kidnapped him aboard their ship. Then grapevines twined around the mast, and the god turned into a lion and sprang at the captain. The terrified sailors leaped into the sea and became dolphins; only the helmsman, who had recognized him as a god from the start, was spared.

Ariadne, princess of Crete, helped Theseus escape the Labyrinth, but he sailed off and left her alone on the shore of the island of Dia. Dionysus found the abandoned, weeping Ariadne and made her his wife. To make her name live forever, he set the crown she wore in the sky, and its jewels became the stars of the constellation Corona Borealis.

Pentheus, the young king of Thebes, refused to accept his cousin Dionysus as a god and tried to lock up the women who followed him. Disguised as a stranger, Dionysus appeared before the king and miraculously slipped free of his chains, then lured the king into spying on the women reveling on Mount Cithaeron. But once on the mountain, Pentheus was mistaken for a wild beast by his mother and the other women, gripped by god-sent madness, and was killed.

myth-013.summary: Quiet goddess who tends the hearth fires of homes and temples.
facts: The eldest daughter, she was the first child Cronus swallowed and the last he spat back out.
In Rome, the fire in the Temple of Vesta was tended by six virgin priestesses.
stories: Both Poseidon and Apollo asked Hestia to marry them, but she laid her hand on Zeus’s head and swore to remain a virgin forever. Instead of marriage, Zeus granted her the place at the center of every home and the choicest portion of every sacrifice. That is why the Greeks always made their first offering to Hestia whenever they sacrificed.

According to the historian Diodorus, Hestia was the goddess who first taught people how to build houses. In gratitude for this gift, people are said to have set aside a place for her in nearly every home and honored her there. In Plato’s writings, too, Hestia alone stays behind in the house of the gods, keeping her place, while the other gods ride out across the heavens in procession.

myth-014.summary: Lord beneath the earth, who rules over the realm of the dead.
facts: Because he granted the minerals and grain that come from the ground, he was also called Pluton, meaning “the wealthy one.”
Pluto, the English name of the dwarf planet, is his Roman name.
stories: With Persephone in his chariot, Hades raced toward the underworld past the lakes of Sicily and its sulfur-reeking marshes. When the spring nymph Cyane rose from the water and blocked his way, declaring that he could not become Demeter’s son-in-law by force, Hades flew into a rage. He hurled his scepter deep into the spring, the earth split open to reveal a road to the underworld, and he drove his chariot down into it and vanished.

Theseus and his friend Pirithous descended to the underworld to carry off Hades’ wife, Persephone. Pretending to welcome them, Hades seated them on the Chairs of Forgetfulness, and the moment they sat down, they stuck fast and could not move. Heracles later came and rescued Theseus, but Pirithous was never set free.

Hades watched the number of dead arriving in the underworld dwindle day by day as the physician Asclepius kept curing the sick. Complaining that his kingdom would suffer if this went on, Hades went before Zeus and accused Asclepius. The enraged Zeus struck Asclepius down with a thunderbolt, according to the historian Diodorus.

myth-015.summary: Goddess of spring who was carried off to the underworld and became its queen.
facts: Because she ate pomegranate seeds, she had to spend a third of every year in the underworld.
In the Eleusinian Mysteries, she was worshipped alongside her mother under the name Kore, meaning “maiden.”
stories: As Persephone was picking flowers in a meadow, the earth split open, and Hades appeared in his chariot and carried her off to the underworld. Anyone who ate the food of the underworld could never return to the world above, and before leaving, Persephone ate pomegranate seeds that Hades had secretly slipped her. So even after returning to her mother, she had to go back down to the underworld for a few months every year.

Smitten with the beauty of the newborn Adonis, Aphrodite hid the baby in a chest without the other gods knowing and left it with Persephone. But when Persephone saw the baby in the chest, she too fell for him and refused to give him back. Zeus settled the goddesses’ quarrel by dividing Adonis’s year into three: one part to spend on his own, one with Persephone, and the rest with Aphrodite.

According to Ovid, Persephone was strolling in the garden of the underworld when she picked a pomegranate and ate seven seeds, and the only one who saw her was Ascalaphus. Because he told on her, Persephone could never fully return to the world above. Furious, Persephone sprinkled him with water from the river Phlegethon, and Ascalaphus’s head turned into a beak and sprouted huge eyes as he became an owl, the bird of ill omen.

myth-016.summary: Young god who shoots arrows that make anyone they hit fall in love.
facts: Cupid, shown as a baby with a bow on Valentine’s Day cards, is his Roman form.
Golden arrows kindle love, while blunt lead arrows drive it away.
stories: Sent by his mother, Aphrodite, to make Psyche fall in love with a worthless man, Eros is said to have pricked himself with his own arrow and fallen in love with her instead. He had the west wind, Zephyrus, carry Psyche to his palace, and later, when she fell into a deathlike sleep, he went to her, lifted the sleep away, and woke her. Then, at Eros’s pleading, Zeus gave Psyche ambrosia to make her a goddess and approved their marriage.

To help Jason, Aphrodite went to find Eros, who was playing a game with Ganymede in Zeus’s orchard. Promising him a beautiful ball that Zeus had played with as a child, the goddess told him to shoot an arrow into the heart of Medea, princess of Colchis. Struck by Eros’s arrow, Medea fell deeply in love with Jason and resolved to defy her father and help him.

Aphrodite summoned Eros, complaining that Hades, ruler of the underworld, was the only one who had yet to yield to the power of love. Eros picked the sharpest and surest of all his arrows and shot it into Hades’ heart. Struck by the arrow, Hades fell in love with Persephone the moment he saw her and carried her off to the underworld, Ovid tells us.

myth-017.summary: Winged goddess who heralds victory in war and in contests.
facts: A headless statue of her, found on the island of Samothrace in 1863, stands atop the Daru staircase in the Louvre.
The sportswear company Nike is named after her, using the English pronunciation of her name.
stories: Before the war with the Titans, when Zeus promised honors to any god who took his side, Nike was the first to come to Olympus, along with her mother, Styx, and her siblings. From then on, Nike never stayed anywhere Zeus did not lead and was always at his side. The poet Bacchylides sang that Nike stands beside Zeus on golden Olympus and judges the outcome of contests of skill between gods and mortals.

When the monster Typhon trampled the heavens, Nike appeared before Zeus in the form of Leto and urged him to take up his thunderbolt and defend Olympus. At the height of the battle, Nike raised a shield in front of Zeus to protect him from Typhon’s attacks. When Zeus finally won, Nike drove his chariot at his side, cracking the heavenly whip, as the poet Nonnus sang.

myth-018.summary: Sun god who drives a fiery chariot across the sky every day.
facts: The Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was a bronze statue modeled on him.
Helium, an element first discovered in sunlight, takes its name from his, which is the Greek word for the sun.
stories: Helios swore by the river Styx to grant his son Phaethon anything he wished, and when the boy asked to drive the sun chariot, Helios tried hard to talk him out of it but could not stop him. He anointed his son’s face with sacred oil to protect him from the flames, but Phaethon could not control the horses and was struck down by Zeus’s thunderbolt. When the grieving Helios refused to drive the chariot ever again, the gods gathered to plead with him, and he took up the reins and set out across the sky once more.

When the gods drew lots to divide the world, Helios was absent and received no land. Zeus offered to draw lots again, but Helios said he had seen land rising from beneath the sea and asked for that island instead. The island that rose above the waves was Rhodes, and Helios took the island’s nymph, Rhodos, as his partner and fathered seven sons with her.

Overcome by hunger, Odysseus’s men ignored the warning not to touch them and slaughtered and ate Helios’s cattle on the island of Thrinacia. Hearing the news from his daughter, Helios demanded that Zeus punish them, or else he would go down to the underworld and shine among the dead. Zeus shattered their ship with a thunderbolt in the middle of the sea, and only Odysseus survived.

myth-019.summary: Moon goddess who drives a silver chariot across the night sky.
facts: Pausanias wrote that she bore Endymion fifty daughters.
Selenium, discovered in 1817, was named after the Moon to pair it with tellurium, which had been named after the Earth.
stories: Selene fell in love with the shepherd Endymion as he slept on Mount Latmus. Endymion fell into an eternal sleep in which he would never age or die; some say Selene asked Zeus for this, others that Endymion chose it himself. Selene is said to have come down to the mountain every night to visit him as he slept.

One story holds that the Nemean lion, the first beast Heracles fought, originally fell from the Moon. The poet Epimenides sang that Selene, at Hera’s bidding, shook herself and flung the savage lion down onto the land of Nemea. Hyginus wrote that Selene raised the lion in a cave with two entrances.

myth-020.summary: Goddess of the dawn, who rises before the sun and paints the sky red.
facts: Homer often called her “rosy-fingered Dawn.”
The aurora, the light that shimmers across polar night skies, takes its name from her Roman name, Aurora.
stories: Eos loved Tithonus, a prince of Troy, and begged Zeus to make him immortal. But she forgot to ask that he never grow old, so Tithonus could not die and simply aged without end. One story says he finally shriveled up until only his voice remained, and he became a cicada.

Eos’s son Memnon went to aid Troy and was killed by Achilles. When the grieving Eos fell at Zeus’s knees and pleaded, the ashes of Memnon’s funeral pyre turned into a flock of birds and flew up, and these birds are said to fight one another every year in his memory. Eos still weeps for her son, and her tears, it is said, are the morning dew that covers the whole world.

Eos fell for the hunter Cephalus as he was setting nets for deer on Mount Hymettus, and she carried him off. But Cephalus longed only for his wife, Procris, and talked of nothing but her. Angered, Eos sent Cephalus back to his wife, warning that one day he would regret having won her.

myth-021.summary: God who drove out his father with a sickle and led the Titans.
facts: Goya’s “Saturn Devouring His Son,” painted on a wall of his house, hangs in the Prado Museum.
The planet Saturn and the English word Saturday both come from his Roman name, Saturn.
stories: When Gaia called on her children to punish their father, Uranus, they all fell silent in fear; only Cronus stepped forward to take on the task. Cronus lay in wait, and when Uranus came down at nightfall, he struck his father with a great sickle his mother had made, drove him out, and became king of the gods. But once on the throne, he locked the Cyclops brothers and the hundred-handed giants, whom his siblings had freed, back in Tartarus, and took his sister Rhea as his wife.

Told by a prophecy that he was fated to lose his throne to one of his children, Cronus swallowed each child Rhea bore. When the youngest, Zeus, was born, Rhea handed him a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes instead, and Cronus gulped it down without suspicion. Later, tricked into it, Cronus vomited his children back up; the stone, swallowed last, came out first and was set up at Delphi.

Cronus was secretly meeting Philyra, a daughter of Oceanus, behind Rhea’s back when Rhea caught them. He turned into a long-maned horse and galloped away. Overcome with shame, Philyra went far off into the mountains, where she gave birth to Chiron, one of the Centaurs, half horse and half god.

myth-022.summary: The goddess who is the Earth itself, mother of all gods and living things.
facts: She bore the sky god on her own, then took him as her mate and gave birth to the twelve Titans.
Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis, which views the Earth as a single living organism, borrows her name.
stories: When Zeus locked the Titans away in Tartarus, an enraged Gaia stirred up the Giants, the Gigantes, to attack Olympus. A prophecy said the gods alone could not kill the Giants, so Zeus called on the mortal Heracles to fight alongside them. When even this war was lost, Gaia gave birth to her last and most terrifying monster, Typhon.

On the day Zeus and Hera were married, Gaia brought a branch bearing golden apples as a wedding gift. Hera was so taken with the apples that she asked for the tree to be planted in the garden of the gods, far away beside Mount Atlas. The tree was guarded by a hundred-headed dragon, and Heracles was later given the labor of fetching its apples.

The hunter Orion once boasted before Artemis and Leto that he could kill any beast the earth had ever produced. Angered, Gaia is said to have sent a scorpion that struck Orion down. Zeus placed the scorpion among the stars as well, which is why, it is said, Orion still sets whenever Scorpius rises.

myth-023.summary: The first god of the sky, who took the earth goddess as his mate.
facts: Of the eight planets, only Uranus is named after a Greek god rather than a Roman one.
The element uranium, discovered by Klaproth in 1789, was named after the planet Uranus, which had been found eight years earlier.
stories: Uranus found the one-eyed Cyclops and the hundred-armed giants born to Gaia so hideous that he shoved them deep inside the earth. Racked with pain from carrying her children within her, Gaia put a sickle in the hand of her son Cronus and plotted revenge. From the blood of Uranus, slashed by the sickle of Cronus, the Furies were born, and from the foam around his flesh that fell into the sea rose Aphrodite.

Uranus called the sons who had raised their hands against him and done this terrible deed Titans, warning that one day they would pay for it. Later, he and Gaia told Cronus that he was fated to lose his throne to his own son. When their daughter Rhea came to them for help in saving her youngest child, the two gods revealed everything to come and sent her to Crete to give birth to Zeus.

myth-024.summary: A goat-legged god who roams the woods and pastures playing reed pipes.
facts: The word “panic,” meaning sudden terror, comes from his name.
The panpipes, an instrument made of pipes of different lengths bound together, are named after him.
stories: Syrinx, a nymph of Arcadia, loved to hunt like Artemis and wanted to live alone. When Pan chased her, she begged her sisters, the river nymphs, to change her shape at the riverbank, and all Pan caught was a handful of reeds. Charmed by the sound of the wind passing through them, Pan joined reeds of different lengths with wax to make a pipe and named it the syrinx.

Before the Battle of Marathon, the Athenian messenger Pheidippides met Pan while running to Sparta. Pan complained that the Athenians neglected him, saying he had helped Athens many times already and would help again. After Athens defeated the Persians, the people built a shrine to Pan in a cave beneath the Acropolis and honored him there.

On Mount Tmolus, Pan was showing off his piping to the nymphs when he boasted that even Apollo's music could not match his pipes. He challenged Apollo to a contest with the mountain god Tmolus as judge, and his simple tune on the wax-bound reed pipes delighted King Midas, who happened to be there. But when Apollo played his lyre, Tmolus ruled that Pan must admit his pipes had lost to the lyre.

myth-025.summary: The goddess of chance who hands out good and bad fortune to mortals.
facts: She is shown holding a horn of plenty and wearing a crown shaped like city walls.
The English word “fortune” comes from her Roman name, Fortuna.
stories: According to Plutarch, Tyche abandoned Persia and Assyria, flitted lightly over Macedonia, and wandered through Egypt and Syria handing out kingdoms here and there. But as she approached Rome's Palatine Hill and crossed the Tiber, the goddess took off her wings, removed her sandals, and even set down the unreliable ball she always rolled about on. And so, it is said, Tyche entered the city meaning to stay in Rome for a long time.

The Romans said that Fortuna loved Servius Tullius, their sixth king. Every night the goddess slipped into the palace through a small window, which is why that opening came to be called the Fenestella, meaning “little window.” The statue of Servius in Fortuna's temple had its face covered by a robe, and one story says the goddess covered it out of shyness.

The Romans told of a time when the goddess Fortuna spoke aloud in a human voice. The women who had saved Rome by persuading Coriolanus's army to withdraw pooled their money to set up a statue of the Fortuna of Women, and the moment it was placed in the temple, it said, “Women, the gods are pleased with your pious offering of me.” Plutarch wrote that Fortuna's voice was heard not once but twice.

myth-026.summary: Apollo's son, who learned healing from a centaur and could even raise the dead.
facts: The Hippocratic Oath begins with a vow sworn by Apollo, by him, and by his two daughters.
His serpent-entwined staff appears on the flag of the World Health Organization.
stories: Asclepius received the blood of the Gorgon from Athena, and the blood drawn from her right-side veins could bring the dead back to life. With it he is said to have revived many, including Hippolytus, the son of Theseus. Fearing that mortals would learn his art and save one another from death, Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt, and a furious Apollo killed the Cyclops who had forged it.

Asclepius learned from the centaur Chiron how to cure every illness that plagues mankind. He healed each patient by the right method, whether they suffered from festering sores, wounds from bronze weapons or slingstones, or bodies harmed by summer heat or winter cold. Pindar sang that he cured people with gentle incantations, soothing potions, salves, and the surgeon's knife.

When a terrible plague struck Rome, the Romans followed the advice of the oracle at Delphi and sent envoys to Epidaurus to bring Asclepius back. The god appeared as a huge serpent and boarded the Roman ship, reaching the coast of Italy six days later and sailing up the Tiber. When the serpent slid onto an island in the middle of the river and returned to his true form, the plague that had gripped Rome vanished without a trace.

myth-027.summary: The goddess of magic who watches over the night and the crossroads.
facts: On the dark night at the end of each month, people would leave out food for her where three roads met.
In “Macbeth,” she appears as the leader who summons and scolds the three witches.
stories: When Persephone was carried off to the underworld, the only ones who heard her screams were Hecate, in her cave, and the sun god Helios. Hecate took up a torch and set out with Demeter to search for the girl, and from Helios, who sees everything, they learned that the culprit was Hades. After Persephone returned, Hecate became her constant companion.

When the Giants, the Gigantes, came to attack Olympus, Hecate joined the battle on the side of the gods. According to Apollodorus, as each god took on a Giant, Hecate defeated the Giant Clytius with the torch in her hand. The Gigantomachy frieze on the Pergamon Altar also shows a triple-bodied Hecate facing Clytius with a torch, a sword, and a spear.

myth-028.summary: The goddess who sparked a quarrel by tossing a golden apple inscribed “To the fairest” into a feast.
facts: Hesiod said there is also a separate, good Eris who spurs people to compete through hard work.
In 2006, her name was given to the dwarf planet that set off the debate leading to Pluto's demotion.
stories: Every god was invited to the wedding of the sea goddess Thetis and the hero Peleus except Eris. Furious, Eris threw a golden apple inscribed “To the fairest” into the feast. When Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed it as her own, Zeus passed the judgment on to the Trojan prince Paris.

Zeus sent Eris down to the Greek ships, holding a portent of war in her hands. Standing on Odysseus's ship in the middle of the camp, she let out a loud, piercing cry that carried to both ends of the line. The cry filled the hearts of the Greek soldiers with strength, and fighting suddenly seemed sweeter to them than sailing home.

As the Trojans and Greeks clashed, Ares and Athena each spurred on one side, and beside them Eris raged without rest. Sister and companion of Ares, she reared her head only a little at first, but soon grew until her head touched the sky as she strode across the earth. Weaving among the soldiers, Eris hurled strife into the midst of both armies, and the groans of men grew louder across the battlefield.

myth-029.summary: The god of sleep, whose mere touch puts anyone to sleep.
facts: He is the twin of Thanatos, god of death, and lives in a cave through which Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, flows.
The English word “hypnosis” comes from his name.
stories: During the Trojan War, Hera asked Hypnos to put Zeus to sleep so she could help the Greeks. Having once been in serious trouble for lulling Zeus to sleep, Hypnos refused at first, but changed his mind when she promised him the goddess Pasithea as his wife. He turned into a bird, hid in a tree, and sent Zeus into a deep sleep.

Hera sent Iris to the god of sleep so that a dream could carry news to Alcyone, who was anxiously awaiting her husband Ceyx, drowned at sea. In a home reached by neither sunlight nor the crowing of roosters, with poppies crowding the cave's entrance, the god of sleep barely opened his eyes and nodded drowsily as he listened. He sent Morpheus, the best mimic of humans among his thousand sons, and then sank back into deep sleep.

The poet Licymnius sang that Hypnos, god of sleep, was deeply in love with the beautiful shepherd Endymion. Wanting to gaze into Endymion's shining eyes forever, Hypnos put him to sleep but left his eyes wide open. The poem survives today because Athenaeus quoted it in his book.

myth-030.summary: The god of death, who carries off those who have drawn their last breath.
facts: Together with the god of sleep, he carried the body of the fallen Sarpedon home to Lycia.
The English word “euthanasia” means “good (eu) death (thanatos).”
stories: Thanks to Apollo, King Admetus could go on living if someone agreed to die in his place, and his queen, Alcestis, volunteered. When Thanatos arrived on the appointed day, Apollo tried to stop him, but Thanatos would not back down and took the queen away. Heracles, who happened to be staying in the house, caught Thanatos at the tomb, wrestled him, and brought Alcestis back.

Thanatos came to take Sisyphus, who had betrayed a secret of Zeus, but the crafty Sisyphus tied him up tightly instead. While the god of death was held captive, no one in the world died. In the end, it is said, Ares, the god of war, came to set Thanatos free and handed Sisyphus over to him.

myth-031.summary: Three goddesses who set each person's lifespan by spinning, measuring, and cutting a thread.
facts: Clotho spins the thread, Lachesis measures it, and Atropos cuts it.
Atropa, the scientific name of the poisonous plant belladonna, and the drug atropine both come from Atropos.
stories: When Althaea, queen of Calydon, gave birth to her son Meleager, the three Moirai came to see the baby. Clotho said the child would be noble, and Lachesis said he would be brave. But Atropos looked at a log blazing in the hearth and decreed that the child would live only until it had burned away.

When the monster Typhon fled to Mount Nysa with Zeus in pursuit, the Moirai came up with a trick. The goddesses coaxed Typhon into believing that a certain fruit would make him even stronger, and Typhon believed them and ate it. But it was the “ephemeral fruit,” whose power lasts only a day, and so, it is said, the goddesses of fate fooled the monster completely.

When the Giants, the Gigantes, hurled boulders and blazing oak trees at the gods of heaven, the Moirai joined the fight too. The three goddesses who always spun, measured, and cut thread took up bronze clubs this one time. According to Apollodorus, the Moirai swung those clubs and struck down the Giants Agrius and Thoas.

myth-032.summary: Nine sisters who inspire poetry, song, and learning.
facts: The words “museum” and “music” both come from them.
Each had her own domain: Calliope for epic poetry, Clio for history, Urania for astronomy, and so on.
stories: As Hesiod was tending his sheep at the foot of Mount Helicon, the Muses appeared before him. Scolding shepherds of the field for caring only about filling their bellies, the goddesses plucked a fresh branch to give him as a staff and breathed a divine voice into him. They then told him to sing of what had been and what was to come, and of the eternal gods, a story told at the opening of the “Theogony.”

The nine daughters of Pierus challenged the Muses to a singing contest. When the sisters kept mocking the goddesses even after losing, the Muses turned them into noisy, chattering magpies. The Roman poet Ovid tells of this contest in the “Metamorphoses.”

The Thracian singer Thamyris boasted that he would win even if the Muses themselves sang against him. The angry Muses defeated him in a contest, then blinded him and took away his gift of song. Homer sang in the “Iliad” that afterward Thamyris even forgot how to play the lyre.

myth-033.summary: The Titan who stole fire and gave it to humanity.
facts: Chained to a rock, he had his liver torn at by an eagle every day.
His name means “he who thinks ahead.”
stories: When Zeus hid fire from mankind, Prometheus secretly stole a spark, hiding it inside the hollow stalk of a fennel plant. He brought the fire to humans, and its far-shining light blazed among them once again. Seeing this, Zeus flew into a rage and decided to punish both humanity and Prometheus.

On the day gods and mortals divided up the sacrifice, Prometheus slaughtered an ox and split it into two portions. In one he hid the meat inside the stomach, and in the other he covered the bones with glistening fat. Zeus saw through the trick but still chose the fat-covered portion; from then on, people ate the meat and burned the bones for the gods, and the angry Zeus took fire away from humans.

Prometheus is said to have mixed earth with water and shaped humans in the likeness of the gods. According to Ovid, while other animals hang their heads and look only at the ground, he made humans stand upright so they could lift their faces to the sky. The traveler Pausanias saw two large stones at Panopeus in Phocis that smelled like human skin, and the locals said they were clay left over from when Prometheus made the human race.

myth-034.summary: The Titan condemned to hold up the sky on his shoulders.
facts: Ovid wrote that he turned to stone on seeing Medusa's head and became the Atlas Mountains.
Mercator named his book of maps after him, and the Atlantic Ocean, too, means “Sea of Atlas.”
stories: According to Hyginus, Atlas was the leader of the Titans when they fought against Zeus. When the defeated Titans were imprisoned in Tartarus, Zeus singled out Atlas for a punishment of his own: to bear the dome of the sky on his shoulders. Hesiod sang that he stands at the ends of the earth, before the land of the Hesperides, holding up the broad sky with his head and tireless arms.

When Heracles came seeking the golden apples, Atlas left the sky in his hands for a while and picked three apples from the garden of the Hesperides. Free of his heavy burden for the first time in ages, he did not want to take up the sky again and offered to deliver the apples to Eurystheus himself. But when Heracles asked him to hold the sky just while he put a pad on his head, Atlas set down the apples and took back the sky, and Heracles picked up the apples and walked off.

In a story told by the historian Diodorus, Atlas was a king who ruled a coastal land, called his people the Atlantians, and gave his own name to the highest mountain. He studied the stars more deeply than anyone, and was the first to teach people that the heavens form a sphere, the celestial sphere. Diodorus explained that the tale of Atlas holding the sky on his shoulders arose as a metaphor for his discovery of the celestial sphere.

myth-035.summary: The first woman, who opened a forbidden jar and unleashed misfortune on the world.
facts: The phrase “Pandora's box,” meaning a source of trouble best left untouched, comes from her story.
It became known as a box because in the 16th century Erasmus translated “jar” as “box.”
stories: To punish humans for stealing fire, Zeus had Hephaestus shape a woman out of clay. Each of the gods gave her a gift, from beauty and a way with words to a cunning mind, and she was called Pandora, meaning “the one who received all gifts.” When Pandora lifted the lid of the jar, disease and sorrow poured out into the world, and when she hastily closed it, only hope remained inside.

myth-036.summary: Greece's mightiest strongman, who carried out twelve labors.
facts: As the son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene, he was hated by Hera all his life.
The English word “Herculean,” meaning extremely difficult, comes from his Roman name.
stories: For his first labor, Heracles tracked down the Nemean lion and shot it with arrows, but even arrows could not pierce its hide. Club in hand, he chased the lion into a cave with two entrances, blocked one, and went in through the other. Heracles wrapped his bare arms around the lion's neck and choked it to death, then carried it on his shoulders back to Mycenae.

For his fifth labor, Heracles had to clear the dung piled up in the stables of King Augeas of Elis in a single day. Without mentioning that it was one of his labors, he struck a deal with the king to receive a tenth of the herd if he finished the job in a day. Heracles broke through the stable walls to make a channel, then diverted the nearby Alpheus and Peneus rivers to rush through and wash the filth away.

When Heracles was eight months old, Hera sent two huge serpents to his bed to kill him. His mother, Alcmene, screamed for her husband Amphitryon, but baby Heracles sprang up and strangled the serpents with his bare hands. Another version says Amphitryon put the snakes there himself to find out which child was his own son.

myth-037.summary: The hero who beheaded a monster by looking only at her reflection in his shield.
facts: Every year in mid-August, shooting stars shower down from the direction of his constellation.
He is the son of Danaë, princess of Argos, and Zeus, who came to her as a shower of gold.
stories: Polydectes, king of Seriphos, wanted Danaë for himself, so he ordered her son Perseus to bring back the head of Medusa. Perseus snatched the single eye and single tooth shared by the Graeae sisters to make them reveal where the nymphs lived, and from the nymphs he obtained winged sandals and a helmet of invisibility. Guided by Athena and watching only the reflection in his bronze shield, he cut off the head of the sleeping Medusa.

When Cassiopeia, queen of Ethiopia, boasted that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, Poseidon sent a flood and a sea monster to ravage the land. Following an oracle, Princess Andromeda was chained to a rock by the shore as an offering to the monster. Perseus, passing by, was promised the princess's hand in marriage, killed the monster, and saved Andromeda.

In the middle of the wedding feast of Perseus and Andromeda, Phineus, who had been engaged to the princess first, burst in with an armed band. Perseus swung his sword and fought off many foes, but there were too many of them and he was slowly driven into a corner. Shouting to his friends to turn their faces away, he held up Medusa's head, and two hundred attackers, along with Phineus as he begged for his life, all turned to stone.

myth-038.summary: The hero who unwound a ball of thread as he entered a labyrinth and slew the monster inside.
facts: The Ship of Theseus paradox, which asks whether a ship with every part replaced is still the same ship, comes from his ship.
He forgot to switch to white sails, so his father threw himself into the sea, which became known as the Aegean after him.
stories: The Cretan princess Ariadne fell in love with Theseus, asked Daedalus how to get out of the Labyrinth, and gave Theseus a ball of thread. Theseus tied one end of the thread at the entrance, went in, killed the Minotaur with his fists, and followed the thread back out. But on the voyage home he forgot to hoist white sails, and his father, Aegeus, seeing the black sails and thinking his son was dead, threw himself into the sea.

On his way to Athens, Theseus defeated one by one the villains who preyed on travelers. Among them was Procrustes, who laid his guests on a bed and killed them, cutting off their legs if they were too tall or stretching them if they were too short. Theseus laid him on that very bed and punished him in exactly the same way.

When Theseus had grown into a young man of both strength and wisdom, his mother, Aethra, led him to a huge rock under which his father had hidden tokens. Theseus put his shoulder to the rock, lifted it with ease, and took out the sword and sandals that lay beneath. His grandfather and mother begged him to take the safe sea route, but, according to Plutarch, Theseus, who had secretly long admired the courage of Heracles, chose the overland road teeming with bandits and set out for Athens.

myth-039.summary: The king who came up with the trick of the wooden horse and wandered for ten years before reaching home.
facts: The English word “odyssey,” meaning a long, adventurous journey, comes from his name.
Homer's “Odyssey” tells the story of his homecoming.
stories: When the walls of Troy would not fall, Odysseus came up with the idea of a great wooden horse and had Epeius build it. He had fifty of the bravest warriors hide inside the horse and ordered the rest of the army to burn their tents and withdraw to wait off the island of Tenedos. When the Trojans dragged the horse, inscribed as an offering from the Greeks to Athena, into the city, Odysseus and the warriors climbed down ropes at night and opened the gates.

When Odysseus returned to his home on Ithaca after twenty years, disguised as a beggar, the one who recognized him at a glance at the palace gate was his old dog, Argos. Inside the palace, suitors were draining his wealth in hopes of winning his wife, Penelope. When Penelope announced she would marry whoever could use her husband's bow to shoot through the holes of twelve axes, the beggar drew the bow that no one else could even string, made the shot, and revealed who he was.

Before sailing past the island of the Sirens, Odysseus did as Circe had told him and plugged his men's ears with wax. Wanting to hear the song himself, he had them tie him firmly to the mast and told them to bind him even tighter if he begged to be freed. When the Sirens sang, promising to tell him everything, he signaled to be let loose, but his men tied him tighter and sailed safely past the island.

myth-040.summary: The Trojan War warrior who could not be wounded anywhere except his heel.
facts: The Achilles tendon at the back of the heel is named after him.
At the wish of his mother, Thetis, he hid in the royal palace on the island of Scyros dressed as a girl.
stories: After losing Patroclus, Achilles returned to battle, drove the Trojan soldiers back inside their walls, and faced Hector, who stood alone before the gate. Hector was wearing Achilles' own armor, taken from Patroclus, and Achilles drove his spear into a gap at the neck that the armor did not cover. Having struck Hector down, he cried out that they had slain the enemy champion whom the Trojans revered like a god, and called for his men to sing a song of victory as they returned to the ships.

After Hector died, his father, King Priam of Troy, was guided by Hermes to Achilles' tent at night. The old king kissed the hands that had killed his son and begged Achilles to think of his own father, Peleus, waiting for him at home. The two men wept together, and Achilles returned Hector's body and promised to halt the fighting while the funeral was held.

As fighting raged over the body of Patroclus, Achilles, who had no armor, went out by the will of the gods and stood at the edge of the trench. Athena cast the aegis around his shoulders and raised a golden cloud and flames above his head, and Achilles gave three mighty shouts from the trench. At the sound, the Trojan soldiers and their horses fell back in terror, and in that moment the Greeks safely recovered the body of Patroclus.

myth-041.summary: Leader of an expedition that set sail in search of the Golden Fleece.
facts: The expedition is known as the Argonauts, after the name of their ship, the Argo.
The golden ram whose fleece he sought is said to have risen into the sky to become Aries.
stories: When Jason asked for the Golden Fleece, King Aeetes of Colchis told him to yoke a pair of fire-breathing, bronze-hoofed bulls and sow a dragon's teeth. Jason rubbed his body with Medea's potion, which protected him from fire and iron for a day, and mastered the bulls. When armed warriors sprang up from the ground where the teeth were sown, he threw a stone among them from a distance to make them fight one another and then cut them all down.

After Medea lulled the dragon to sleep with her potion, Jason, following her advice, seized the Golden Fleece from the oak tree where it hung. The fleece glowed like a cloud reddened by the rising sun, flushing his cheeks and brow like fire. Jason threw the fleece, which reached from his neck to his feet, over his left shoulder, then gathered it up in both hands and hurried back to the ship, anxious that someone might snatch it away.

Raised in the cave of the centaur Chiron, Jason turned up in his hometown of Iolcus at the age of twenty, carrying two spears and wearing a leopard skin. He stood before King Pelias, who had been warned by an oracle to beware a man wearing only one sandal, and demanded that the king return the scepter and throne, though he could keep the flocks and fields. When Pelias gave him the task of bringing back the Golden Fleece, Jason immediately sent out heralds to gather heroes for the expedition.

myth-042.summary: A musician whose lyre playing enchanted even wild beasts and rocks.
facts: He is said to have been torn apart by Thracian women who worshipped Dionysus.
In 1607, Monteverdi's opera “L'Orfeo” brought his story to the stage.
stories: When his wife Eurydice died of a snakebite, Orpheus passed through the gate at Taenarum and went down to the underworld. His song moved even the Furies to tears for the first time, and the king of the underworld agreed to give his wife back on condition that he not look back. But just short of the world above, Orpheus turned around, and Eurydice, with only a word of farewell, vanished back into the underworld.

Orpheus, son of the Muse Calliope, is said to have enchanted even hard mountain rocks and flowing rivers with his songs. Drawn by the sound of his lyre, oak trees followed him down from Pieria and stood in rows at Zone on the coast of Thrace, it is said. On the advice of the centaur Chiron, Jason welcomed Orpheus as a member of the Argonauts.

One night, as the Argonauts were feasting on the shore, Idas and the seer Idmon began to quarrel, and Orpheus took up his lyre in his left hand and began to sing. He sang of how earth, sky, and sea, once mingled together, were separated; how the stars, mountains, and rivers came to be; and how Cronus was followed by the young Zeus. Spellbound by his song, the heroes forgot their quarrel and listened, and when it ended, they poured offerings of wine to the gods and went to bed.

myth-043.summary: The craftsman who designed a labyrinth from which no one could escape.
facts: He made wings of wax and feathers and escaped from Crete with his son.
One theory holds that the intricate layout of the Palace of Knossos gave rise to the legend of the Labyrinth.
stories: At the command of Minos, Daedalus built a labyrinth to imprison a monster. He wove countless passages that twisted and overlapped like the winding Maeander River to deceive the eye. The Labyrinth was so complex, it is said, that once it was finished, even Daedalus, who built it, could barely find his way back to the entrance.

Daedalus fled the kingdom of Minos on wings, flew north, and landed on the heights of Cumae. As soon as he touched the ground, he dedicated his wings to Apollo and built a vast temple, carving the death of Androgeos and the story of the Cretan Labyrinth onto its doors. But when he tried to carve the fall of his son Icarus in gold, twice his hands trembled and he could not finish, as Virgil sang.

To find the runaway Daedalus, Minos offered a great reward to anyone who could pass a thread through a spiral seashell. Daedalus, hiding in a royal palace in Sicily, solved the puzzle by boring a hole in the tip of the shell and sending in an ant tied to a thread. When Minos received the answer, he knew at once that Daedalus was there.

myth-044.summary: A boy who flew too close to the sun until his wings melted and he fell.
facts: In the painting traditionally attributed to Bruegel, all you can see of him is two legs sticking out of the sea.
The asteroid Icarus, which swings closer to the Sun than Mercury does, is named after him.
stories: Minos imprisoned Daedalus and his son Icarus so they could not leave Crete. Daedalus bound bird feathers together with thread and wax to make two pairs of wings, warning that flying too low would soak them with seawater and flying too high would let the sun melt the wax. Drunk on the joy of flight, Icarus climbed higher and higher until his wings came apart and he plunged into the sea.

Pausanias tells a version in which Icarus escaped Crete with his father not on wings but in a small boat. Thanks to sails, a new invention of his father's, they outran Minos's fleet, but Icarus handled his rudder clumsily and his boat capsized. His body washed up on an island opposite Samos, where Heracles recognized and buried him, and the island and the surrounding sea came to bear his name.

myth-045.summary: A prince who escaped burning Troy and made his way to Italy.
facts: Julius Caesar's family, the Julii, claimed descent from his son Iulus.
He is the hero of Virgil's epic poem the “Aeneid.”
stories: On the night the Greeks set Troy ablaze, Aeneas carried his aged father Anchises on his shoulders out through the flames. Anchises clutched the family's household gods, young Iulus held his father's hand, and Aeneas's wife Creusa followed behind. But Creusa was lost along the way, and when Aeneas went back to search for her, her ghost appeared and told him his destiny lay in a land to the west.

When Aeneas sought to visit his father in the Underworld, the Sibyl told him he must first find the golden bough, an offering for Persephone. Guided by two doves sent by his mother Venus, he obtained the bough, which only someone favored by fate could break off. In the paradise of the Underworld, Anchises showed him the descendants to come, such as Romulus, who would found Rome, and Augustus.

Arriving in Italy, Aeneas fought a final duel with Turnus, king of the Rutuli, for the land of Latium. He hurled his spear with all his might and brought Turnus down, and he hesitated for a moment as his enemy begged for his life, but when he saw the sword belt of young Pallas, an ally Turnus had killed, he ended the fight. Livy relates that Aeneas married Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus, and named his newly founded city Lavinium after her.

myth-046.summary: Troy's eldest prince, who fell to Achilles while defending the city.
facts: The English verb “hector,” meaning to bully with loud bluster, comes from his name.
The funeral held after his body is returned brings the “Iliad” to a close.
stories: At the gate in the wall the Greeks had built to protect their ships, Hector hoisted a pointed boulder that two strong men of today could barely budge. Zeus made the stone light for him, and he hurled it into the center of the gate, smashing the hinges, snapping the bars, and bursting the doors wide open. Gripping two spears, Hector charged through and called the Trojans in after him, and the Greeks fled toward their ships.

Hector challenged any Greek to meet him in single combat, and Great Ajax, chosen by lot, stepped forward. The two traded spear thrusts and stones in an even fight until nightfall, when heralds stepped in to stop it. Praising his opponent's courage, Hector gave him his sword, Ajax gave him his belt in return, and they parted like friends.

As Achilles closed in, Hector panicked and fled three times around the walls of Troy. Then Athena appeared in the guise of his brother Deiphobus, offering to fight at his side, and Hector found the courage to turn and stand his ground. But after hurling his spear, he looked around and his brother was nowhere to be seen; realizing a god had tricked him, he fought on to the end and fell.

myth-047.summary: The Trojan prince who had to choose the most beautiful of three goddesses.
facts: He picked Aphrodite over Hera and Athena and won Helen of Troy as his prize.
He brought down Achilles with an arrow to the heel.
stories: While tending sheep on Mount Ida, Paris had to decide who was the most beautiful of Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, whom Hermes had brought to him. Hera promised him a kingdom ruling over all people, Athena victory in war, and Aphrodite marriage to Helen of Troy. Paris chose Aphrodite and promptly set sail for Sparta, where Helen lived, on a ship built by Phereclus.

Arriving in Sparta, Paris became King Menelaus's guest and was lavishly entertained for nine days. When Menelaus left for Crete to bury his maternal grandfather, Paris persuaded Queen Helen to run away with him. They slipped away by night with a great deal of treasure aboard, and according to the story, a storm raised by Hera even drove them as far as Sidon.

Raised as a shepherd, Paris entered the games at Troy to win back his favorite bull after the king's servants took it as a prize for funeral games. The games honored a prince believed dead, Paris himself, and he won every event, beating even his own brothers, the princes. Furious, Deiphobus drew his sword, and Paris leapt onto the altar of Zeus, where Cassandra recognized who he was, and he was restored as a prince.

myth-048.summary: The king of Mycenae who led the allied Greek army to Troy.
facts: On the day he returned home, he was murdered by his wife Clytemnestra.
The gold mask Schliemann found at Mycenae in 1876 was named after him, though it is actually older.
stories: In the tenth year of the Trojan War, forced to give back the daughter of a priest of Apollo, Agamemnon took Briseis, the woman who was Achilles' prize, in her place. Insulted, Achilles withdrew from the fighting and shut himself in his tent. Without their greatest warrior, the Greeks suffered defeat after defeat, and it is with this very quarrel that the “Iliad” begins.

The Greek fleet bound for Troy was stranded at the port of Aulis with no wind. The seer Calchas declared that Agamemnon had angered Artemis by shooting a deer and boasting of his skill, and that the king must sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia. Agamemnon lured her there with the lie that she would marry Achilles, but the moment she stood on the altar, Artemis is said to have put a deer in her place and carried the girl away.

Clad in gleaming armor, Agamemnon fought at the front and cut down Trojan warriors one after another, including Bienor and Isus and Antiphus, two sons of Priam. He drove the fleeing Trojans past the tomb of Ilus right up to the Scaean Gates. Even after Coön, seeking to avenge his brother, speared him in the arm, Agamemnon killed him, and only when the wound began to throb did he finally withdraw in his chariot.

myth-049.summary: A hero of Corinth who tamed the winged horse with a golden bridle from Athena.
facts: He defeated the Chimera by attacking it from the sky above.
The insignia of the United Kingdom's airborne forces shows him riding Pegasus.
stories: Seeking to be cleansed of the crime of killing his brother, Bellerophon went to Proetus, king of the land of Argos. But Queen Stheneboea fell for him and asked to meet him in secret, and when he refused her, she turned the tables and told her husband he had tried to assault her. Unwilling to harm a guest with his own hands, the king sent him to his father-in-law, Iobates, king of Lycia, carrying a letter that asked for the bearer to be killed.

Bellerophon struggled to tame Pegasus, but the winged horse would not let him near. As he slept beside an altar of Athena, the goddess appeared in a dream and handed him a golden bridle, and when he awoke, the bridle really was in his hand. He slipped it over Pegasus as the horse drank at the spring of Peirene, and the horse let him climb on without a fight.

When Bellerophon returned after slaying the Chimera, Iobates, king of Lycia, sent him against the fierce Solymi, and then against the Amazons. When he still came back alive, the king picked the bravest warriors in Lycia to ambush him, but Bellerophon defeated them all. Only then, impressed by his courage, did the king give him his daughter Philonoe in marriage and, on his death, leave him the kingdom.

myth-050.summary: He solved a riddle to become king of Thebes, then blinded himself on learning he had killed his father and married his mother.
facts: He answered that the creature with one voice that walks on four feet, then two, then three is man.
Sigmund Freud named a son's attraction to his mother after him.
stories: Warned by an oracle that he would die at his son's hands, King Laius of Thebes pierced his newborn son's ankles with a brooch and had a herdsman abandon him. The baby, left on Mount Cithaeron, was found by the cowherds of King Polybus of Corinth and brought to Queen Periboea, who raised him as her own. The queen healed his ankles and named him Oedipus, meaning “swollen foot.”

When plague struck Thebes, Oedipus sent Creon to Delphi and received an oracle: the killer of the former king, Laius, must be found. He swore to track down the culprit and questioned, one after another, the seer Tiresias, a messenger from Corinth, and an old shepherd. When he finally learned that the killer was he himself, Oedipus put out his own eyes and begged to be sent away from the land.

The oracle at Delphi told Oedipus he would kill his father and marry his mother. Believing the king and queen of Corinth who had raised him to be his real parents, he left home to escape his fate. But the old man he killed in a quarrel on the road was his real father, Laius, and step by step the prophecy he had tried to flee came true.

myth-051.summary: A monster with snakes for hair who turned anyone who met her eyes to stone.
facts: Of the three Gorgon sisters, she was the only one who could die.
The logo of the fashion brand Versace is her face.
stories: Medusa lived with her two sisters in the land of the Gorgons at the edge of the world, and according to Ovid, its fields and roadsides were full of people and animals turned to stone by her face. When Perseus arrived, Medusa was fast asleep along with the snakes of her hair, and he cut off her head; from her blood sprang the winged horse Pegasus. Her two sisters awoke and gave chase, but they never caught sight of Perseus, who wore the helmet of Hades.

According to the Roman poet Ovid, Medusa was originally a maiden famous for her beautiful hair. But when Poseidon violated her in Athena's temple, the enraged Athena turned Medusa's hair into snakes. From then on, it is said, anyone whose eyes met Medusa's was turned to stone.

According to Ovid, Medusa's head kept its astonishing power even after it was cut off. As Perseus flew over the deserts of Libya carrying the head, the drops of blood that fell became all kinds of snakes, and when he set it down on seaweed by the shore, the soft seaweed hardened like stone. Delighted, the sea nymphs tried it with other seaweed and spread it through the sea, and this, it is said, was the origin of coral.

myth-052.summary: A monster with a bull's head and a man's body, kept in the labyrinth of Crete until Theseus killed it.
facts: Apollodorus recorded his original name as Asterius.
Every nine years, Athens sent seven boys and seven girls to be devoured by him.
stories: Locked deep inside the labyrinth built by Daedalus, the Minotaur fed on young people from Athens, chosen by lot and sent every nine years. According to Plutarch, the youths who entered the labyrinth were either killed by the Minotaur or wandered lost until they died, unable to find the way out. After devouring two such tributes, the Minotaur was finally slain by Theseus, who came with the third.

Minos promised Poseidon he would sacrifice a white bull that had come out of the sea, but he coveted it and sacrificed another bull instead. The angry Poseidon made Queen Pasiphae fall in love with the white bull, and the child born of that union was the bull-headed Minotaur. Minos had Daedalus build the labyrinth to imprison the monster and fed it seven young men and seven maidens sent as tribute from Athens.

myth-053.summary: The three-headed dog that guards the gate of the Underworld.
facts: In 2013, one of Pluto's small moons was named after him: Kerberos.
Spellbound by Orpheus's song, he froze with all three mouths hanging open.
stories: For the last of his twelve labors, Heracles had to bring Cerberus up to the world above. Hades agreed he could take the dog if he caught it with his bare hands, using no weapons. Though bitten by the serpent on its tail, Heracles wrapped his arms around the dog's head and choked it into submission, then showed it to King Eurystheus before sending it back to the Underworld.

Cerberus was a fearsome dog guarding the palace of Hades, king of the Underworld, and Persephone. According to Hesiod, he fawned on those entering the Underworld, wagging his tail and both ears. But if anyone tried to pass back out through the gate, he lay in wait, seized them, and devoured them, so that no one who entered could ever return.

When Heracles dragged Cerberus up to the surface, the dog, startled by the blinding sunlight, thrashed wildly and sprayed white foam over the fields. According to Ovid, the foam soaked into the ground and grew into aconite, a deadly poisonous plant. Later, Medea is said to have tried to kill young Theseus with this poison when he came to Athens.

myth-054.summary: A marsh-dwelling water serpent that grew two new heads for every one cut off.
facts: Heracles' nephew Iolaus seared the severed necks with fire so they could not grow back.
Its middle head could not be killed, so it was pinned under a boulder.
stories: The Hydra lurked in a hillside den beside the spring of Amymone at Lerna until fiery arrows shot by Heracles drove it out. It coiled around one of Heracles' feet and clung on, and every time he smashed a head with his club, two new ones sprouted in its place. Finally, Iolaus seared the stumps of the necks with a torch so no more heads could grow, and even the immortal central head was cut off and buried under a heavy boulder by the roadside.

Raised in the swamps of Lerna, the Hydra came out onto the plains and trampled livestock and land alike. According to Hyginus, its venom was so potent that its breath alone could kill a person. Even people who merely passed by the sleeping Hydra were said to breathe in the poison lingering in its tracks and die in agony.

While Heracles fought the Hydra, Hera sent a giant crab to bite his foot. Heracles crushed the crab underfoot, killed the Hydra, and dipped his arrowheads in its venomous blood, while the crab rose into the sky to become the constellation Cancer. These poisoned arrows later brought down many enemies, but in the end they also cost Heracles his own life.

myth-055.summary: A fire-breathing monster that was lion, goat, and serpent joined in one body.
facts: In biology, an organism made of cells with different genes is called a chimera.
An ancient bronze statue of the Chimera, unearthed at Arezzo in 1553, is now in a museum in Florence.
stories: The Chimera had the forequarters of a lion and the tail of a dragon, and breathed fire from a goat's head in the middle of its body. Raised by a man named Amisodarus, the Chimera ravaged the fields of Lycia and preyed on herds, bringing disaster to many. With the strength of three beasts in one body, it is said, it could not easily be overcome even when many people attacked it at once.

Iobates, king of Lycia, received a letter from his son-in-law asking him to kill his guest, Bellerophon. Unable to harm a guest directly, the king gave him the task of slaying the Chimera, which was burning the country. Bellerophon rose into the sky on Pegasus and thrust a lead-tipped spear into the monster's mouth, and it is said the lead, melted by the Chimera's own fire, sealed its throat.

myth-056.summary: A monster on the road to Thebes that posed a riddle and devoured anyone who couldn't solve it.
facts: Unlike the Sphinx at Giza in Egypt, she had wings and a woman's face.
In the Boeotian dialect she was called Phix, and Mount Phikion took its name from her.
stories: Sent by Hera, the Sphinx sat on a rock outside Thebes and posed a riddle to passersby. When everyone who failed to answer had been devoured, Thebes proclaimed that whoever rid the city of the monster would receive the throne and the queen's hand. Oedipus solved the riddle, the Sphinx threw herself to her death, and as promised he became king and married Queen Jocasta.

Apollodorus says the Sphinx was born of the monsters Echidna and Typhon. Armed with a riddle she had learned from the Muses, she settled on Mount Phikion near Thebes. Countless Thebans lost their lives for failing to answer, among them Haemon, the son of Creon.

The Sphinx perched on a rugged cliff between two hills not far from Thebes, glaring out over the plain. According to the Roman poet Statius, whenever a traveler who faced her riddle failed to answer, she instantly bared her sharp claws and teeth and lunged, beating her wings fearsomely. Even after the Sphinx was gone, it is said, herds of cattle and flocks of sheep would not go near the meadow beside that cliff.

myth-057.summary: Sea monsters whose songs lured sailors onto the rocks.
facts: Ancient Greeks pictured them with birds' bodies and women's heads; the fish tail became popular in the Middle Ages.
The alarm called a siren and the woman in the Starbucks logo both take their name from them.
stories: Sitting in a flowery meadow, the Sirens bewitched passing sailors with high, clear songs, and around them lay heaps of bones of those who, spellbound, never made it home. They were fated to die if anyone ever heard their song and sailed past unharmed. When the wily Odysseus heard their song and still sailed safely past the island, the Sirens are said to have thrown themselves into the sea.

According to Pausanias, the Sirens, urged on by Hera, challenged the Muses to a singing contest. But it was the Muses who won. The goddesses then plucked the defeated Sirens' feathers and made crowns from them for their own heads.

According to Ovid, the Sirens were originally daughters of the river god Achelous who had been picking flowers with Persephone. When Persephone was carried off to the Underworld, they searched every corner of the land and prayed for the power to search over the sea as well. The gods granted their wish and gave them birds' wings and feet, but left their beautiful faces and voices unchanged.

myth-058.summary: A race of giants with a single round eye in the middle of the forehead.
facts: They also appear as the smiths who forged Zeus's thunderbolts.
Odysseus told Polyphemus his name was “Nobody,” then put out the giant's eye.
stories: Driving his flock home to his cave, the one-eyed giant Polyphemus sealed the entrance with a boulder so huge that twenty-two wagons could not have moved it, trapping Odysseus and his men. At every meal he seized two of the men and ate them, and each morning he moved the boulder aside as easily as one lifts the lid of a quiver, then put it back. Even after losing his eye, he tore off a mountaintop and hurled it at the fleeing ship, and the wave it raised swept the ship back toward the shore.

Polyphemus, the one-eyed giant of Sicily, loved the sea nymph Galatea, but her heart belonged to a young man named Acis. Seeing the two together by the shore, Polyphemus, burning with jealousy, tore a rock from Mount Etna and hurled it, crushing Acis beneath it. Grief-stricken, Galatea turned his blood flowing from under the rock into clear water, bringing Acis back as a river god.

The Greeks believed the Cyclopes had built the massive walls that still stand at Tiryns and Mycenae. The traveler Pausanias wrote that the walls of Tiryns were made of unworked stones, the smallest of which could not be budged by a pair of mules. These walls were said to have been built by the Cyclopes for King Proetus, and walls like them are still called Cyclopean masonry today.

myth-059.summary: A winged white horse born from Medusa's blood.
facts: The constellation Pegasus, a great square in the fall evening sky, depicts him.
The red winged-horse logo of the oil company Mobil depicts him.
stories: Puffed up after slaying the Chimera, Bellerophon tried to ride Pegasus all the way up to Olympus, home of the gods. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse, and the startled Pegasus bucked, throwing Bellerophon to the ground. Pegasus went on alone to Olympus and became the horse that carries Zeus's thunderbolts.

When the Muses held a singing contest with the daughters of Pierus on Mount Helicon, the mountain, enraptured by the Muses' song, swelled up toward the heavens. At Poseidon's bidding, it is said, Pegasus kicked the summit with his hoof to stop it. Where his hoof struck, a spring gushed forth: the Hippocrene, whose name means “horse's spring.”

myth-060.summary: A race that is human from the waist up and horse from the waist down.
facts: They are usually portrayed as wild, but Chiron was a wise teacher.
Of the 88 constellations, two take this form: Sagittarius and Centaurus.
stories: Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, invited the Centaurs as guests to his wedding. But drunk on wine, the Centaurs tried to carry off the bride and the other women, and the feast turned into a battlefield. Seen as a clash between civilization and savagery, this fight was carved into the sculptures of the Parthenon.

The centaur Chiron was a wise teacher who raised heroes in his cave on Mount Pelion. He took in the infant Achilles and fed him the innards of lions and wild boars and the marrow of bears, and according to Pindar, from the age of six Achilles was killing lions and boars and bringing them back to his teacher. Chiron taught medicine to Asclepius, and Jason is said to have grown up in his cave for twenty years.
