The centaur Nessus ferried travelers across the Evenus River for a fee, claiming the gods had granted him the right. While carrying Heracles' wife Deianira across, he tried to make off with her, and Heracles, hearing her scream, shot an arrow into his chest. As he lay dying, Nessus tricked Deianira into believing that if she kept some of his blood, she could keep her husband's love.

myth-061.summary: A six-headed monster that snatched sailors from ships passing through a narrow strait.
facts: Her home was thought to be the Strait of Messina, between Sicily and mainland Italy.
The English phrase “between Scylla and Charybdis” means being caught with no good way out.
stories: Following Circe's advice, Odysseus steered his ship away from the whirlpool and toward the rock where Scylla lived. While everyone stared in dread at the whirlpool on the opposite side, Scylla stretched out her six heads and snatched six sailors at once. Odysseus later recalled the sight of them crying out his name as they were carried off as the most pitiful thing he had seen in all his wanderings at sea.

Even after a jealous Circe's poison herbs turned her lower body into a pack of savage dogs, Scylla never left the strait. Nursing her grudge, she seized her chance for revenge on Circe by snatching Odysseus's companions. Later she would have sunk the Trojans' ships too, but before she could, she was turned to stone and became a reef that sailors still steer clear of.

Scylla was a savage monster who lived in a cave above the strait, scouring the sea for prey, and she is said to have stolen and eaten some of the cattle of Geryon that Heracles was driving. For this, the enraged Heracles killed her. But her father, the sea god Phorcys, is said to have brought her back to life by burning her flesh with torches.

myth-062.summary: A whirlpool monster that gulped down the sea and spat it out again, swallowing ships.
facts: She was said to suck down the sea three times a day.
Odysseus survived by clinging to a fig tree on the cliff.
stories: After a storm wrecked his ship, Odysseus drifted all night clinging to the mast and keel, and Charybdis tried to swallow him once more. As she gulped down the sea, mast and keel and all, Odysseus hung like a bat from a fig tree on the cliff and barely held on. Long afterward, when Charybdis spewed the timbers back up, he dropped onto them and escaped.

Charybdis was the daughter of Poseidon and Gaia, notorious for an appetite that devoured everything. When she stole and ate cattle that Heracles was driving, an angry Zeus hurled a thunderbolt and cast her into the sea. From then on, Charybdis became a whirlpool beneath the sea, endlessly swallowing water and spewing it out.

When Odysseus and his men first entered the strait, Charybdis was sucking down the sea with terrifying force. When she spewed the water out, it seethed like a cauldron over a roaring fire, flinging spray to the tops of both cliffs; when she swallowed it, the rocks roared horribly and the black sand of the seabed lay bare. The sailors went pale at the sight and could not take their eyes off Charybdis.

myth-063.summary: Monsters with birds' bodies and women's faces that swooped in to snatch away food.
facts: Their name means “snatchers” in Greek.
The harpy eagle, a large bird of prey of Central and South American forests, takes its scientific name Harpia from them.
stories: Whenever the seer Phineus, who had rashly revealed the will of Zeus, tried to eat, the Harpies swooped down from the clouds, snatched away his food, and left a foul stench on whatever remained. When Zetes and Calais, sons of the North Wind, chased them with swords drawn, the Harpies fled over the sea faster than the West Wind. Iris, goddess of the rainbow, stopped the brothers by swearing the Harpies would never trouble Phineus again, and the Harpies withdrew to a cave on Crete.

Aeneas and his men landed on the Strophades and held a feast of cattle and goats they had caught in the meadows. Then the Harpies flew in, snatching and fouling the food, and however the men swung their swords, not a single feather was harmed. Their leader, Celaeno, perched on a rock and cursed them: even if they reached Italy, they would not build walls around their city until hunger drove them to gnaw their own tables.

Podarge, one of the Harpies, was grazing in a meadow by the stream of Oceanus when she bore two horses to Zephyrus, god of the west wind. These were Xanthus and Balius, immortal steeds as swift as the wind. The pair later drew the chariot of the hero Achilles and were also yoked to it when his friend Patroclus rode into battle.

myth-064.summary: The largest and fiercest of all monsters, who sent even the gods running.
facts: Defeated by Zeus's thunderbolts, he is said to lie pinned beneath the volcano Mount Etna in Sicily.
Some say the English word “typhoon” traces back to his name.
stories: Typhon grappled with Zeus, cut the sinews of his hands and feet with a sickle, and locked him away in a cave. Hermes and Aegipan secretly stole the sinews back and fitted them into Zeus again. Back on his feet, Zeus drove Typhon off with a barrage of thunderbolts and at last hurled Mount Etna in Sicily on top of him, pinning him beneath it.

Typhon was taller than the mountains, his head brushing the stars, and when he stretched out his arms, one hand reached the far west and the other the far east. Fire flashed from his eyes and flames poured from his mouth as he hurled red-hot rocks at the sky and charged heavenward with a roar. Terrified, the gods fled to Egypt and changed themselves into animals to hide from him as he gave chase.

According to Hesiod, a hundred snake heads sprouted from Typhon's shoulders, and they made every kind of sound, from the speech of the gods to the bellowing of bulls, the roaring of lions, and the barking of dogs. Typhon very nearly became master of gods and mortals alike, but Zeus's thunderbolts set all his heads ablaze, and he fell and was hurled into Tartarus. Hesiod sings that the savage winds that scatter ships and ruin fields come from this very Typhon.

myth-065.summary: A beautiful youth who fell in love with his own reflection in the water and wasted away.
facts: A narcissus flower is said to have bloomed in the spot where he had been.
Narcissism, meaning self-absorption, comes from his name.
stories: When Narcissus was born, the seer Tiresias said he would live a long life if he never came to know himself. As he grew up, many fell in love with him, but he gave his heart to no one, and the goddess Nemesis answered the prayer of one he had spurned. Coming to a spring tired from hunting, Narcissus became captivated by his own reflection in the water, could not tear himself away, and wasted away there.

myth-066.summary: A nymph who loved Narcissus in vain until her body faded away and only her voice remained.
facts: As punishment from Hera, she lost the power to speak first.
Her name itself means “echo” in Greek, and the English word echo is the same word.
stories: Whenever Zeus was off with the other nymphs, the nymph Echo would keep Hera occupied with endless chatter. When Hera realized she had been tricked, she made Echo able only to repeat the last words of others. Later, Echo fell in love with Narcissus, but unable to tell him how she felt, she pined away until only her voice remained.

Separated from his companions in the woods, Narcissus called out, “Is anyone here?” and Echo answered, “Here!” When he said, “Come, let us meet,” Echo joyfully replied, “Let us meet!” and rushed out of the woods to throw her arms around him. Narcissus pushed her away and fled, and in her shame, Echo hid herself in deep forests and caves.

Echo still harbored anger toward Narcissus for rejecting her, but when she saw him wasting away by the spring, she pitied him. Each time he sighed “Alas,” Echo sighed “Alas” too, and when he said a last “Farewell” and died, Echo answered “Farewell.” When the water nymphs wept for him, Echo returned their cries and mourned along with them.

myth-067.summary: The king of Phrygia who asked Dionysus to make everything he touched turn to gold.
facts: There was also a real Phrygian king named Midas in the 8th century BC, who appears in Assyrian records as Mita.
The tale of the donkey ears Apollo gave him closely resembles the Korean folktale “The King's Ears Are Donkey Ears.”
stories: When some farmers caught Silenus and brought him in, Midas treated him lavishly for ten days and then returned him to Dionysus. The delighted god offered him a wish, and Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold, but even his bread and wine became gold, leaving him unable to eat or drink. Regretting his mistake, he followed the god's instructions and bathed at the source of the Pactolus River to wash the power away, and ever since, the river's sands have glittered gold.

At a music contest between Pan and Apollo, Midas alone insisted that Pan's piping was better. Furious, Apollo turned his ears into donkey's ears, and Midas went about hiding them under a cap. His barber discovered the secret and, unable to keep it any longer, dug a hole in the ground and whispered it in; the reeds that grew on that spot spread the words every time the wind blew.

Midas is said to have captured Silenus by mixing wine into a spring to get him drunk. He pressed Silenus on what was best for humankind, and Silenus, who had kept his lips tightly sealed, finally gave in to the relentless questioning. The least painful life, Silenus answered, is one lived unaware of one's own misery, and the best thing for a human is never to have been born at all.

myth-068.summary: The king of Corinth condemned to push a boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down every time.
facts: He is said to have been punished for tattling on one of Zeus's secrets and even for chaining up the god of death.
Albert Camus reinterpreted his endless, futile labor in “The Myth of Sisyphus.”
stories: Facing death, Sisyphus told his wife in advance not to give him a funeral. Once in the underworld, he complained that she had failed to honor him with proper rites and won permission to return briefly to the world above, supposedly to scold her. But he never went back, living on until he died of old age, and for that he was sentenced to roll a boulder uphill for all eternity.

When Zeus carried off Aegina, daughter of the river god Asopus, her father searched far and wide until he came to Corinth. Sisyphus knew the culprit was Zeus, but refused to say until Asopus gave him a spring at the top of the Corinthian hill. Once he had his spring, Sisyphus revealed the truth; Asopus chased after Zeus, was struck by a thunderbolt, and was driven back into his own riverbed.

The thief Autolycus changed the color and horn shape of whatever cattle he stole, so Sisyphus could never find his missing cows. Suspicious that his own herd kept shrinking while Autolycus's kept growing, Sisyphus secretly carved marks into his cattle's hooves. When Autolycus stole cattle again, Sisyphus went to him, picked out his own animals by the marks on their hooves, and took every one of them back.

myth-069.summary: The king doomed to stand forever with water and fruit right before his eyes, never able to reach them.
facts: His son Pelops lives on in the name of the Peloponnese, the peninsula in southern Greece.
The English word “tantalize” and the element tantalum both come from his name.
stories: Tantalus was a king so favored that he dined at the same table as the gods, yet he killed his son Pelops and served him to them as a meal. Some say he wanted to test whether the gods truly knew everything; most of them saw through it and refused to touch the dish, but Demeter, distraught over the loss of her daughter, ate a shoulder. The gods brought Pelops back to life and replaced his shoulder with ivory, and Tantalus was condemned to eternal hunger and thirst in the underworld.

The poet Pindar refused to believe that Tantalus cooked his son for the gods, dismissing it as a tale invented by envious neighbors. In his telling, Tantalus's real crime was stealing the nectar and ambrosia the gods had given him to make him immortal and sharing it with his drinking companions. As punishment, Zeus hung a huge boulder over his head.

On Crete, the goat that nursed the infant Zeus was guarded, at Rhea's command, by a golden dog. Pandareus stole the dog and left it with Tantalus, who later swore he had never received any such dog and feigned ignorance. Enraged, Zeus turned Pandareus to stone on the spot and, it is said, struck Tantalus with a thunderbolt and pinned him beneath Mount Sipylus.

myth-070.summary: A young woman of Lydia who challenged Athena to a weaving contest and was turned into a spider.
facts: Angered by a tapestry that depicted the gods' misdeeds, the goddess struck her with a weaving shuttle.
Her name means “spider” in Greek, and the class Arachnida comes from the same word.
stories: Proud of her weaving, Arachne boasted that she was better even than Athena. Athena, disguised as an old woman, warned her to stop, but she wouldn't listen, and the two ended up holding a weaving contest. When Arachne flawlessly wove the gods' wrongdoings into her cloth, the furious goddess tore it apart, and Arachne became a spider, doomed to spin thread forever.

In her contest with Athena, Arachne wove in stories of gods who had changed their shapes to deceive mortals. Zeus as a bull carrying Europa across the sea, Zeus as a swan, Zeus as a shower of gold: each scene seemed real enough to move, and she bordered the cloth with flowers and ivy. Her work was so perfect that even Athena could not find a single flaw in it.

Arachne came from no famous family; she was the daughter of an ordinary dyer in Colophon who dyed wool purple. Even so, her weaving was renowned throughout Lydia, and nymphs left the vineyards of Mount Tmolus and the waters of the Pactolus River to flock and watch her work. People said she must have learned her craft from Athena, but Arachne denied it and boasted that she would take on the goddess herself.

myth-071.summary: A sculptor of Cyprus who fell in love with the ivory statue of a woman he had carved himself.
facts: Aphrodite breathed life into the statue, which later came to be called Galatea.
The Pygmalion effect, the idea that high expectations actually improve performance, takes its name from this story.
stories: Disappointed in the women around him, Pygmalion, a sculptor on Cyprus, resolved to live alone. He carved a woman out of ivory more beautiful than any living one, then dressed the statue and brought it gifts, cherishing it like a real lover. On the day of Aphrodite's festival he prayed for a wife like his statue, and when he came home and kissed it, the cold ivory grew warm and came to life.

myth-072.summary: The most beautiful woman in the world, whose fate sparked the Trojan War.
facts: The daughter of Leda and Zeus, who had taken the form of a swan, she was queen of Sparta before going to Troy.
“The face that launched a thousand ships” is a line by the English playwright Christopher Marlowe.
stories: In Troy, Helen was embroidering a great purple cloth with scenes of the fighting between Trojans and Greeks that she herself had caused. Hearing that Paris and Menelaus were to duel over her, she climbed atop the city gate and pointed out the Greek commanders beyond the walls to King Priam, one by one. As she named Agamemnon, Odysseus, and Ajax the Great, she wept with regret at having left her daughter and her homeland behind.

After the wooden horse was hauled inside Troy, Helen went to it with Deiphobus, circling it three times and running her hands over it. She called out the names of the Greek commanders hidden inside, one by one, imitating the voice of each man's wife. When one of the deceived warriors started to answer, Odysseus clamped his hand over the man's mouth, and the Greeks only narrowly escaped discovery.

myth-073.summary: The primordial gap at the very beginning, when nothing existed, from which everything is said to have come.
facts: Ovid pictured it as a shapeless mass in which all the elements were jumbled together.
The word “chaos,” meaning disorder, and even the word “gas” come from this name.
stories: Hesiod's “Theogony” sings that first of all, Chaos came into being. Next appeared broad-breasted Gaia, the earth; deep Tartarus; and Eros, the god of love. From Chaos were born Erebus, the darkness, and Nyx, the night, and these two in turn bore the bright upper air and the day, as the world gradually took shape.

The Roman mythographer Hyginus wrote that Chaos was born from mist. According to him, Chaos gave birth to Nyx (night), Hemera (day), Erebus (darkness), and Aether, the bright air of the heavens. Whereas Hesiod made the day and the upper air grandchildren of Chaos, Hyginus portrayed all four as Chaos's own children.

myth-074.summary: The goddess who was night itself, whom even Zeus dared not cross.
facts: Hesiod sang that Night and Day pass each other at a bronze threshold: as one comes in, the other goes out.
Pluto's moon Nix is named after this goddess.
stories: Nyx was a mother who bore countless children all on her own, without a partner. According to Hesiod, she gave birth to Thanatos, the god of death; Hypnos, the god of sleep; and the tribe of dreams, as well as the Moirai, goddesses of fate, and Nemesis, goddess of retribution. Deceit, Old Age, Eris the goddess of strife, and many other forces that drive the world were born from her as well.

Hypnos, who had put Zeus to sleep at Hera's request, was in deep trouble once the deed came to light. As the furious Zeus was about to hurl him from the sky into the sea, Hypnos fled into the arms of his mother, Nyx. Afraid of offending the goddess of night, Zeus let his anger go.

In a work by the comic playwright Aristophanes, a chorus of birds sings of the world's beginning like this. First of all, black-winged Nyx laid a wind-egg in the bosom of Erebus, the boundless darkness. When its time came, Eros, the god of love, hatched from that egg on golden wings, and after him came the sky, the sea, the earth, and the gods.

myth-075.summary: The primordial sea that the earth goddess bore all on her own.
facts: His name simply means “sea” in Greek.
The ancient Greek name for the Black Sea was Pontos Euxeinos, “the hospitable sea.”
stories: Pontus was the sea that Gaia bore by herself, without a partner. He later paired with Gaia and fathered Nereus, the Old Man of the Sea, along with Phorcys and Ceto, the ancestors of monsters. Nereus's fifty daughters are the sea nymphs known as Nereids, and one of them is Thetis, the mother of Achilles (a different goddess from the Titan Tethys).

According to Hyginus's handbook of myths, Pontus paired with Thalassa, goddess of the sea, and fathered all the tribes of fish. That is why Pontus is spoken of as the father of fish and other sea creatures. A fragment of the ancient epic “Titanomachy” also says that Pontus and Gaia had a son, Aegaeon, who lived in the sea and fought on the Titans' side.

myth-076.summary: An abyss lying even deeper than the underworld, used as a kind of prison.
facts: One theory holds that Europeans spelled the Tatars as “Tartars” partly because the name echoed this one.
It was said that an anvil dropped from the earth would take nine days to fall this far.
stories: After winning the war against the Titans, Zeus imprisoned the defeated Titans in Tartarus. According to Hesiod, it was enclosed by a bronze wall and ringed by night in three layers like a necklace, and its entrance was a set of bronze gates that Poseidon had installed. Inside lived the hundred-armed giants as Zeus's loyal guards, so no one could ever escape.

According to Hesiod, Tartarus was a primordial being who appeared after Chaos first came into being, along with Gaia, the earth, and Eros, the god of love. After Zeus drove the Titans out of the sky, Tartarus lay with Gaia and fathered her youngest monster, Typhon. But Typhon, struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt, was in the end hurled into the wide abyss of his father, Tartarus.

myth-077.summary: The Titan of the great river believed to flow around the edge of the world like a ring.
facts: The English word “ocean” comes from his name by way of Latin.
The giant riding a seashell chariot at the center of Rome's Trevi Fountain depicts him.
stories: When the Titans fought Zeus, Oceanus did not side with his siblings, and Hesiod says his daughter Styx, following her father's wishes, was the first to come over to Zeus. So even after the war he went unpunished, keeping his place flowing around the ends of the world. In a tragedy by Aeschylus, he appears as an old god who visits Prometheus, chained to a rock, and urges him to bow to Zeus.

When Heracles crossed to the island of Erytheia in the far west aboard Helios's golden cup, Oceanus put the hero's nerve to the test. Appearing as a phantom in the middle of the open sea, he tossed the cup carrying Heracles to and fro. Heracles immediately aimed his bow, and the frightened Oceanus cried out for him to stop, according to the early writer Pherecydes.

myth-078.summary: The Titan goddess who, with her partner Oceanus, gave birth to the nymphs of the world's rivers and springs.
facts: The Tethys Ocean, an ancient sea from the age of the dinosaurs, is named after her.
She is a different goddess from Thetis, the sea nymph who was the mother of Achilles.
stories: Tethys paired with the Titan Oceanus and bore the swirling rivers and countless daughters, the Oceanids. Hesiod sang that there were three thousand daughters and as many rivers, and that the daughters, together with Apollo and the rivers, watch over the young across the earth. When Zeus was driving Cronus beneath the earth, Tethys also took the young Hera from Rhea and raised her lovingly in her own home.

Tethys welcomed her foster daughter Hera, who came to her seething after Zeus's beloved Callisto and her son were set in the sky as a constellation. Granting Hera's request, Tethys barred those stars from coming down to bathe in her waters. That, it is said, is why Ursa Major never sinks below the horizon but circles the northern sky all year round.

When the Trojan prince Aesacus, grieving for the nymph he loved, threw himself from a high cliff into the sea, Tethys took pity on him. She caught him gently as he fell and wrapped him in feathers on the waves, saving his life. Turned into a bird, Aesacus kept diving into the water ever after, and Ovid wrote that the bird's name, too, came from its diving.

myth-079.summary: The Titan of light, whose children were the gods of the sun, the moon, and the dawn.
facts: The world's tallest known tree, found in California in 2006, bears his name.
His name means “the one who goes on high” in Greek.
stories: The historian Diodorus wrote that Hyperion was the first Titan to study the heavens closely, working out the movements of the sun, moon, and stars as well as the seasons. That is why he was called the father of the sun and the moon, and Homer sometimes even called his son Helios by the name Hyperion. In William Shakespeare's play, Hamlet compares his late father to Hyperion to honor his noble bearing.

myth-080.summary: The Titan goddess who, with Hyperion, gave birth to the sun and the moon.
facts: Her name means “divine” in Greek.
She lent her name to the hypothetical planet thought to have collided with Earth and formed the Moon.
stories: Theia paired with her brother Hyperion and bore the sun, the moon, and the dawn. The Greek poet Pindar sang that it is thanks to Theia that people value gold above all else. Every dazzling, glittering light was believed to be this goddess's gift.

myth-081.summary: The Titan said to be the pillar of the northern sky and the master of inquiring intellect.
facts: With his sister Phoebe he fathered Leto.
His Latin name, Polus, means the axis of the heavens, and the English word “pole” comes from the same root.
stories: Coeus paired with his sister Phoebe and fathered ever-gentle Leto and Asteria of the lovely name. Leto bore Apollo and Artemis, and Asteria bore Hecate, goddess of magic, which made Coeus the maternal grandfather of three gods. A Homeric Hymn honors his name by calling Leto the most glorious daughter of great Coeus.

myth-082.summary: The Titan goddess said to have handed the Delphic oracle down to her grandson.
facts: The mother of Leto, she was the grandmother of Apollo and Artemis.
Her name means “bright,” and Saturn's moon Phoebe is named after her.
stories: The seat of the Delphic oracle passed from Gaia to Themis and then to Phoebe. When her grandson Apollo was born, Phoebe gave it to him as a birthday gift. That is why Apollo came to be called Phoebus, an epithet taken from her name.

myth-083.summary: The Titan of the southern sky, said to govern the movements of the constellations.
facts: With Eurybia he fathered Astraeus, Pallas, and Perses.
His name means “ram,” and the Greeks called the constellation Aries “Krios.”
stories: Crius is the least distinctive of the Titans; little survives about him beyond his family tree. According to Hesiod, he paired with Eurybia, a daughter of Gaia, and fathered Astraeus, Pallas, and Perses. Astraeus in turn paired with Eos, goddess of the dawn, and fathered the winds, the morning star, and the stars of the sky, making Crius in effect the grandfather of the stars and winds.

myth-084.summary: The Titan father of the brothers Prometheus, Epimetheus, and Atlas.
facts: His name resembles that of Noah's son Japheth, and since ancient times some have identified the two as one figure.
Saturn's moon Iapetus, bright on one side and dark on the other, is named after him.
stories: Iapetus paired with Clymene, a daughter of Oceanus, and had four sons: Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus, and Menoetius. Each of his sons defied Zeus and was either punished or brought disaster on humankind. And since Prometheus's son Deucalion is said to have repopulated the world after the Great Flood, Iapetus is also a distant ancestor of humanity.

myth-085.summary: The Titan goddess of memory, mother of the nine Muses.
facts: Orphic initiates were taught to drink from her spring in the underworld rather than from the river of forgetfulness.
The English word “mnemonic,” meaning a memory aid, shares the same root.
stories: According to Hesiod, Zeus spent nine nights with Mnemosyne in Pieria. A year later she gave birth to nine daughters, the Muses, whose hearts were set on song alone. They were born, Hesiod sang, to help people forget their troubles and find rest from sorrow.

The historian Diodorus wrote that Mnemosyne was the Titan who first discovered how to use the powers of thought and reasoning. She is said to have given names to everything around us, so that people could put what they wanted into words and talk with one another. Because the human power to recall the past was also considered her gift, Diodorus says, her name came from the word for memory.

myth-086.summary: The Titan goddess of divine law, depicted holding scales and a sword.
facts: The statues of Lady Justice outside courthouses carry on her image.
As Zeus's second wife, she bore the goddesses of the seasons and the goddesses of fate.
stories: According to the historian Diodorus, Themis was the Titan who first introduced people to oracles, sacrifices, and the rules for worshipping the gods. She also taught people to obey the law and live peacefully with one another. That is why, the story goes, Apollo's act of giving oracles was called by a word derived from the name of Themis, who first discovered them.

When the Great Flood was over, Deucalion and Pyrrha, the only survivors, went to the temple of Themis and prayed for a way to restore humankind. Themis gave an oracle telling them to cover their heads, loosen their robes, and throw the bones of their great mother over their shoulders. Realizing that the bones were the stones of the earth, the couple threw stones, which turned into people, and a new human race was born.

Zeus and Poseidon both wanted to marry the sea nymph Thetis. Then Themis revealed that the son Thetis bore was destined to become greater than his father. The two gods hastily backed off, and Thetis married the mortal Peleus and gave birth to Achilles.

myth-087.summary: The Titan goddess who, when her husband swallowed their children, handed him a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes in place of her youngest.
facts: She hid her youngest child, Zeus, in a cave on the island of Crete and raised him there.
Her Roman name, Ops, means “abundance” and shares a root with the English word “opulent.”
stories: Rhea hid the infant Zeus in a cave on Crete and left him in the care of nymphs and the goat Amalthea. Whenever the baby cried, young warriors called the Curetes danced and beat their shields with their spears to drown out the sound. Thanks to them, Cronus never found out that his son was alive.

The people of Arcadia say that after giving birth to Poseidon, Rhea hid him among a flock of sheep to grow up with the lambs. She told Cronus she had given birth to a horse and gave him a foal to swallow instead of the baby. According to Pausanias, the spring where the sheep grazed was therefore called Arne, meaning “lamb's spring.”

myth-088.summary: The Titan who forgot his brother's warning and took Pandora as his wife.
facts: His name means “one who thinks too late,” or afterthought.
He handed out every ability to the animals and had nothing left for humans.
stories: Prometheus firmly warned his brother never to accept any gift sent by Zeus. But when Hermes brought the beautiful Pandora, Epimetheus forgot his brother's words entirely and took her as his wife. Only after disaster had spread across the world did he realize what he had let in.

After the gods had shaped animals and humans, Epimetheus begged his brother Prometheus to let him take charge of handing out abilities to them. He gave swift feet to some animals and strength, wings, and thick hides to others, until he had used up everything he had. Seeing humans left naked and defenseless, Prometheus stole fire and craft from Hephaestus and Athena and gave them to humankind.

myth-089.summary: The king of Crete who had a labyrinth built and shut a monster inside it.
facts: After his death, he is said to have become a judge in the underworld.
Arthur Evans, who excavated Knossos in 1900, named the Minoan civilization after him.
stories: According to Diodorus, Minos became king of Crete, founded famous cities such as Knossos, Phaistos, and Cydonia, and issued laws he claimed to have received while conversing with his father, Zeus, in a cave. He built a powerful fleet, subdued most of the islands, and became the first Greek to rule the seas. Thucydides likewise wrote that he drove the Carians out of the Cyclades, installed his sons as governors, and did his utmost to stamp out piracy.

When Minos besieged Megara, Scylla, daughter of King Nisus, watched him from a tower and fell in love with the enemy commander. This princess, who shared only her name with the sea monster, secretly cut off her father's purple lock of hair, which kept the kingdom safe, and offered it to Minos, but he recoiled in horror at her betrayal and cast her aside. When Minos set sail without her, Scylla chased after him and was turned into a seabird.

Pursuing Daedalus all the way to Sicily, Minos demanded that King Cocalus hand him over. The king agreed and invited Minos to bathe, but the king's daughters, who were fond of Daedalus, poured boiling water over him and killed him. Afterward, Minos became a judge of the dead in the underworld.

myth-090.summary: A beast with the head and wings of an eagle and the body of a lion.
facts: Herodotus described it as a beast that guards gold in the far north.
Scania, the truck maker from Sweden, features one in its logo.
stories: The griffin was a beast with a lion-like body and an eagle's beak and wings, said to guard gold in a faraway northern land. According to a poem by Aristeas quoted by Pausanias, griffins fought the one-eyed Arimaspians over gold that welled up from the ground. Herodotus, too, recorded a story that the Arimaspians steal the gold the griffins guard.

The Roman-era writer Aelian wrote that the griffins of India walked on four legs like lions, with black feathers on their backs, red ones on their chests, white wings, and eyes that blazed like fire. Gold came from the barren mountains where they lived, so people in India would sneak in to mine it on moonless nights in bands of a thousand or two thousand. The griffins fought intruders to protect their young, and it is said that a fully grown griffin could never be captured.

According to a sage from India quoted by Philostratus, griffins used their powerful beaks to dig out rocks studded with flecks of gold like sparks. Because griffins were sacred to Helios, the sun god, painters in India depicted him with four griffins pulling his chariot side by side. Though they couldn't fly far, griffins attacked lions and even defeated elephants and great serpents, but they were no match for the tiger, which was as swift as the wind.
